import { Aside, CardGrid, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Your [`#[app::state]`](/build/sdk-macros/) struct is the whole data model of your
app. Every field is a collection from `calimero_storage::collections`: the
storage format your state is written in, and the API you program against. This
page is about choosing those collections, and the patterns that keep an app
correct and fast as it grows.

## How calls see state

An app's calls run one at a time, on its leader, each against the state the
previous one left, and the other replicas apply what it wrote
([CRDT collections](/protocol/crdt-internals/)). Design around four facts:

- **Calls are serialized.** Two members writing the same thing at once do not
  race: the second call runs after the first and sees its write. There is no
  merge between replicas to reason about.
- **You read your own write.** A call's answer carries its log index; a view
  reads the leader's latest state, or a replica's once it has applied that index
  ([Reads](/protocol/reads/)).
- **Anything any member can write, every member can write.** Plain state is
  public to everyone who reaches the app. If a field must be owner-only or
  per-user, you model that with an access-controlled wrapper — see
  [Access-controlled storage](/build/permissioned-storage/).
- **A run is a transaction.** It writes everything or, on an error or a trap,
  nothing.

## Choose the collection for your data

The [Collections](/build/collections/) page is the full reference. The design
question is the shape of the data and how you read it:

| Data | Reach for | What a write does |
|--------|-----------|---------------------------|
| One value | `LwwRegister<T>` | Replaces the value |
| A count | `Counter` / `GCounter` / `PNCounter` | Adds to the executor's slot; the value is the sum |
| A set | `UnorderedSet<V>` / `SortedSet<V>` | Adds or removes one member |
| Key→value | `UnorderedMap<K, V>` / `SortedMap<K, V>` | Writes one entry; a nested collection is its own entity |
| An ordered list | `Vector<V>` | Appends; each push mints a stable element id |
| Collaborative text | `FugueText`, or `RichText` / `RichDocument` for formatting and blocks | Inserts at a character id, so a position stays put while others type |
| Collaborative text an app already stores as RGA | `ReplicatedGrowableArray` | Per-character RGA ordering |

Nesting is the lever you compose with: a
`UnorderedMap<String, LwwRegister<String>>` is "a map where each key is its own
cell" — the pattern `apps/wasmer-fixtures/kv-store` uses. A `UnorderedMap<String, Counter>` is
"a count per key." Each entry is its own entity, so writing one does not rewrite
the others.

<Aside type="caution" title="Bare scalars are rejected">
  You cannot put a bare `String`, `u64`, or `bool` directly in state — the state
  lint rejects it. Wrap it: `LwwRegister<u64>` for a value, `Counter` for a sum
  of increments.
</Aside>

## Shared vs private state

Everything above is **shared** state: it lives in your `#[app::state]` struct,
and every run reads it. `#[app::private]` declares a second kind: the
**caller's private state**, kept in the caller's own space of the app's state
(`env::private_storage_*`). It is replicated and sealed like the rest, but only
runs whose caller is that account read or write it, and app code cannot address
another account's space.

| | Shared state (`#[app::state]`) | Private state (`#[app::private]`) |
|---|---|---|
| Who reads it | Every run | Only runs of the account it belongs to |
| Who writes it | Every member who reaches the app, unless a wrapper restricts it | Only that account's runs |
| Field types | Collections | Plain values: `u64`, `String`, `Vec`, `BTreeMap`, and the structural `UnorderedMap` / `UnorderedSet` / `Vector` (auto-pointed at private storage) |

Because a private space has a single writer, access-control wrappers are
meaningless there, so `#[app::private]` **rejects those types at compile time**:
a `LwwRegister`, `Counter`, `SharedStorage`, `UserStorage`, `FrozenStorage`,
`AuthoredMap`, and friends inside a private struct each produce a targeted
compile error pointing at the plain type to use instead (a `LwwRegister<u64>`
becomes a bare `u64`; a `Counter` becomes a plain integer).

Reach for `#[app::private]` for what is one account's own:

- **Secrets** — a plaintext value where only its hash belongs in shared state.
  The `apps/private_data` game keeps each guess's secret in private state and
  publishes only `sha256(secret)` to the shared map.
- **Per-account bookkeeping** — drafts, preferences, "have I attempted this?"
  sets that no one else needs to read.

The *how* — the typed `private_load` / `private_load_or_default` accessors and the
save-on-drop write pattern — lives on
[Access-controlled storage](/build/permissioned-storage/#the-callers-private-state),
next to the other write-boundary tools.

## A worked domain model: a marketplace

The patterns below are easier to see in one cohesive schema. Here is a small
marketplace, and the modeling decision behind each field:

```rust
#[app::state]
#[derive(Default, BorshSerialize, BorshDeserialize)]
struct Marketplace {
    // Primary store: listing id -> listing. Every access is a point lookup by
    // id and there is no global ordering need, so UnorderedMap (not SortedMap).
    listings: UnorderedMap<String, Listing>,

    // Secondary index: (seller id ++ big-endian seq) -> listing id, a SortedMap
    // you maintain yourself; `prefix(seller)` slices one seller's listings in
    // order without scanning the whole marketplace. `IndexedMap` can keep this
    // for you instead: declare `#[index(seller_created(seller, created_at))]`
    // on `Listing` and query
    // `listings.query("seller_created").eq(&seller).desc()`, which reads it
    // from `listings` itself, so it cannot drift.
    by_seller: SortedMap<Vec<u8>, LwwRegister<String>>,

    // Per-buyer slot: each buyer writes only their own shipping profile; the
    // wrapper refuses anyone else's write.
    buyers: UserStorage<LwwRegister<String>>,
}

#[derive(Default, app::Mergeable, BorshSerialize, BorshDeserialize)]
struct Listing {
    title: LwwRegister<String>,
    price: LwwRegister<u64>,
    sold: LwwRegister<bool>,   // a flag, never a `remove` — see below
}
```

Publishing a listing writes the primary entry **and** its index entry in the
same call, so both land in one entry or neither does:

```rust
listings.insert(id.clone(), listing)?;
let mut key = seller_id.as_bytes().to_vec();
key.extend_from_slice(&seq.to_be_bytes());     // big-endian: keep the index time-ordered
by_seller.insert(key, id.into())?;

// One seller's listings, newest-first, without touching anyone else's:
let theirs = by_seller.prefix(seller_id.as_bytes())?;

// A buyer sets their own shipping address; no other member can overwrite it:
buyers.insert(address.into())?;
```

The decisions worth calling out:

- **`sold` is a flag, not a `remove`.** A sold listing stays readable, with its
  history, for buyers and for disputes — the
  [tombstone pattern](#soft-delete-via-tombstones) below.
- **The index is kept by your code.** A method that edits a listing's seller and
  forgets `by_seller` leaves a stale entry. Write both in every method that
  changes either, or let `IndexedMap` keep the index — the
  [secondary-index caveat](#a-secondary-index-you-maintain-in-a-second-map).
- **Composite key over nesting.** A single `SortedMap` with `seller ++ seq` keys,
  sliced by `prefix`, is simpler than a `UnorderedMap<seller, SortedMap<...>>` and
  needs only one index collection to keep up to date.

The rest of this section unpacks each of these patterns in isolation.

## Patterns &amp; recipes

### Ordered / paginated data with `SortedMap`

`SortedMap` / `SortedSet` are the `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` to the unordered types'
`HashMap`/`HashSet`: the same entries, plus key-ordered reads: `range(a..b)`,
`prefix(p)`, `page(offset, limit)`, `first()`, and `last()`.

The catch: **ordering is byte order over the key**, so your `Ord` must match
`as_ref()` byte order. `String` / `&str` /
`Vec<u8>` sort lexicographically and just work. **Multi-byte integers must be stored
big-endian**, or `255` sorts before `256`:

```rust
// Time-ordered log: big-endian key so range/pagination scan in real order.
let mut log: SortedMap<[u8; 8], LwwRegister<String>> = SortedMap::new();
log.insert(seq.to_be_bytes(), entry.into())?;        // big-endian!
let first_page = log.page(0, 20)?;                    // ascending by key
let window = log.range(start.to_be_bytes()..end.to_be_bytes())?;
```

On a cluster the node keeps no ordered index, so each ordered read sorts the
entries in memory, `O(n log n)`
([Storage performance](/build/storage-complexity/)). `apps/sorted-kv-store`
makes the same ordered reads on the component SDK, where a `Table` keeps its
records in key order.

### Per-user data with `UserStorage`

When each member owns exactly one slot — a profile, a preference, a per-user
cursor — `UserStorage<T>` keys by account automatically. Each account writes only
its own slot; reads are open:

```rust
let mut profiles: UserStorage<LwwRegister<String>> = UserStorage::new();
profiles.insert("Alice".into())?;                     // writes env::account_id()'s slot
let mine = profiles.get()?;                            // my slot
let theirs = profiles.get_for_user(&bob_key)?;         // anyone's slot, read-only
```

A member cannot overwrite another member's slot: the wrapper refuses the write. On
the component SDK the same rule is a table keyed by the caller's account, as in
`apps/kv-store-with-user-and-frozen-storage`.

### An open keyspace with per-entry owners via `AuthoredMap`

When *anyone* may add entries but only the *author* may edit theirs — a shared
catalog, a comment thread, a classifieds board — use `AuthoredMap<K, V>`. Insert is
open and stamps the inserter as owner; `update` / `remove` are owner-only:

```rust
let mut listings: AuthoredMap<String, LwwRegister<String>> = AuthoredMap::new();
listings.insert("listing-42".into(), body.into())?;    // open; caller becomes owner
listings.update(&"listing-42".into(), edit.into())?;    // only the owner succeeds
let owner = listings.owner_of(&"listing-42".into())?;
```

`AuthoredVector<V>` is the same idea for an append-only log: any member pushes, only
the author updates or tombstones their slot.

### Soft-delete via tombstones

When a deleted thing must stay explainable (a listing someone bought, a message
someone replied to), model deletion as state rather than absence:

```rust
struct Note {
    body: LwwRegister<String>,
    deleted: LwwRegister<bool>,   // tombstone flag
}
```

Views filter on the flag, and the entry keeps its id, so references to it stay
valid. `AuthoredVector::tombstone` follows this model (it replaces the slot with
`V::default()` rather than physically removing it, so element ids stay stable).
Use a hard `remove` when nothing refers to the entry.

### Per-user counters

Compose a map of counters when you need "a count per member":

```rust
let mut points: UnorderedMap<String, Counter> = UnorderedMap::new();
points.entry("Alice".into())?.or_default().increment()?;
```

Each `Counter` sums per-executor increments, so `value()` is the total and each
executor's share stays visible.

### A secondary index you maintain in a second map

If you need lookups by a non-primary attribute, keep a second map and write both
in the same call (or let `IndexedMap` do it):

```rust
// Primary: id -> user.  Secondary: email -> id.
users.insert(id.clone(), user)?;
by_email.insert(email, id.into())?;
```

A method that changes the attribute without updating the second map leaves a
stale entry, so confirm index hits against the primary map on read.

## Anti-patterns

### Huge collections under one parent

A single collection with very many direct children gets expensive: every write
touches the parent's child set, and that cost grows with the number of children.
Prefer sharding (e.g. a map keyed by a prefix bucket, or a `SortedMap` you page
through) over one flat collection of hundreds of thousands of entries. See
[Storage performance &amp; Big-O](/build/storage-complexity/) for the exact costs and
how each collection scales.

### `time_now` / randomness in migrations

A call reads `time_now` and `random_bytes` once, on the leader, and the other
replicas apply the result, so a call may use them. A **migration** runs in merge
mode, where the SDK replays writes, so anything there must be a pure function of
the state it reads.

<Aside type="caution" title="Counters and clocks in migrations">
  `Counter::increment` and `Rga::insert` read the executor id / HLC of the *live*
  call and intentionally **panic** in merge mode. Their deterministic siblings —
  `increment_for(device_id)` and `insert_str_at_timestamp(...)` — take the value
  explicitly. `FugueText`, `RichText` and `RichDocument` writes panic the same
  way; seed them with `insert_str_with_replica` and `mark_with_replica`. See
  [migrations](/build/migrations/).
</Aside>

### Reading a replica that is behind

A strong view reads the leader's latest state. A view allowed to read a replica
that is behind (`minIndex`, or `--min-index` in `meroctl`) sees that replica's
applied state: pass the index of your own last write to read it back
([Reads](/protocol/reads/)).
